problems.title: Level 1: Reverse an Array
problems.description: Given an array of integers, reverse the elements and print the result.
problems.starter_code:
# Problem: Reverse an Array (Amazon, TCS Ninja)
# Task: Given an array of integers, reverse the elements and print the result.
# Expected Goal: Reversed: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# TODO: Write your code below to solve this problem:
problems.buggy_code:
arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
rev = []
for i in range(len(arr), 0, -1):
    rev.append(arr[i])
print('Reversed:', rev)
problems.correct_code:
arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
rev = []
for i in range(len(arr) - 1, -1, -1):
    rev.append(arr[i])
print('Reversed:', rev)

precomputed_hints.hint_1: Logic Flaw: When reversing, it is natural to think 'a list with 5 items starts counting back from 5'. But in programming, positions start at 0! A 5-element list only has slots 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Trying to read slot 5 immediately crashes because that position does not exist.
precomputed_hints.hint_2: Core Concept: In zero-indexed languages, the last valid element of any array of length N is always located at index N - 1. When stepping backwards, your starting boundary must be N - 1, and you must continue down until index 0 is processed.
precomputed_hints.hint_3: What to Change in Logic: In Python, change your range to range(len(arr) - 1, -1, -1). In Java, initialize your reverse loop with 'for(int i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)'. This starts at the true last element (index 4) and stops safely after reading the first element (index 0).

cause_explanation.programmer_intent: Solve challenge 'Reverse an Array'.
cause_explanation.actual_execution: Attempted to read arr[length] which is beyond the array boundary.
cause_explanation.divergence_gap: Indices start at 0, so the last valid index is always length - 1.
cause_explanation.prevention_tip: Golden Rule: The last item of any list of size N is at index N - 1.

# Problem: Check if Array is Palindrome (Infosys, Wipro Elite)
# Task: Check whether an array reads the same forward and backward.
# Expected Goal: Is Palindrome: True

# TODO: Write your code below to solve this problem:
problems.buggy_code:
arr = [1, 2, 3, 2, 1]
is_pal = True
for i in range(len(arr)):
    if arr[i] != arr[len(arr) - i]:
        is_pal = False
        break
print('Is Palindrome:', is_pal)
problems.correct_code:
arr = [1, 2, 3, 2, 1]
is_pal = True
for i in range(len(arr)):
    if arr[i] != arr[len(arr) - 1 - i]:
        is_pal = False
        break
print('Is Palindrome:', is_pal)

precomputed_hints.hint_3: What to Change in Logic: Subtract an additional 1 in your mirror index calculation: change arr[len(arr) - i] to arr[len(arr) - 1 - i] in Python, or arr[arr.length - 1 - i] in Java. This accurately matches opposite symmetrical pairs.

cause_explanation.prevention_tip: Golden Rule: Mirror of index i is always at (length - 1 - i).

problems.title: Level 4: Two Sum (Pair with Target Sum)
problems.description: Find two numbers in a sorted array that sum up to target.
problems.starter_code:
# Problem: Two Sum (Pair with Target Sum) (Google, Amazon, Meta)
# Task: Find two numbers in a sorted array that sum up to target.
# Expected Goal: Pair: [2, 7]

nums = [2, 7, 11, 15]
target = 9

# TODO: Write your code below to solve this problem:
problems.buggy_code:
nums = [2, 7, 11, 15]
target = 9
left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1
while left < right:
    s = nums[left] + nums[right]
    if s == target: break
    elif s < target: right -= 1
    else: right -= 1
print('Pair:', [nums[left], nums[right]])
problems.correct_code:
nums = [2, 7, 11, 15]
target = 9
left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1
while left < right:
    s = nums[left] + nums[right]
    if s == target: break
    elif s < target: left += 1
    else: right -= 1
print('Pair:', [nums[left], nums[right]])

precomputed_hints.hint_1: Logic Flaw: When the current sum (nums[left] + nums[right]) is smaller than the target, decrementing right makes the sum even smaller! You need to make the sum larger to reach the target.
precomputed_hints.hint_2: Core Concept: In a sorted array, numbers grow larger as you move from left to right. Moving the left pointer forward (left += 1) increases the sum, while moving the right pointer backward (right -= 1) decreases the sum.
precomputed_hints.hint_3: What to Change in Logic: Inside the elif s < target branch, change 'right -= 1' to 'left += 1'. Keep 'right -= 1' only for when s > target.

cause_explanation.programmer_intent: Solve challenge 'Two Sum (Pair with Target Sum)'.
cause_explanation.actual_execution: When current sum is too small, moving right pointer makes it even smaller.
cause_explanation.divergence_gap: Left pointer controls smaller values; incrementing it increases total sum.
cause_explanation.prevention_tip: Golden Rule: In two-pointer sorted search, sum < target -> left++, sum > target -> right--.

# Problem: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (Microsoft, Adobe)

# TODO: Write your code below to solve this problem:
problems.buggy_code:
nums = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
write = 1
for i in range(1, len(nums) + 1):
    if nums[i] != nums[i - 1]:
        nums[write] = nums[i]
        write += 1
print('Unique count:', write)
problems.correct_code:

precomputed_hints.hint_1: Logic Flaw: You used range(1, len(nums) + 1), which attempts to read nums[len(nums)]. The read pointer walks past the array boundary on the last step.
precomputed_hints.hint_2: Core Concept: The in-place two-pointer technique uses a slow 'write' pointer that records distinct items and a fast 'i' pointer that reads every item. The read pointer must strictly stop before len(nums).
precomputed_hints.hint_3: What to Change in Logic: Change the loop bound to range(1, len(nums)) in Python, or i < nums.length in Java. Every time nums[i] differs from nums[i-1], overwrite nums[write] and advance write.

cause_explanation.programmer_intent: Solve challenge 'Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array'.
cause_explanation.actual_execution: Accessing nums[len] caused IndexError.
cause_explanation.divergence_gap: Loop reached one step past the last element.
cause_explanation.prevention_tip: Golden Rule: Array scanning loops should never touch length index.

problems.description: Compute (base^exp) % mod efficiently in O(log exp) time.
problems.starter_code:
# Problem: Fast Modular Exponentiation (Google, Uber)
# Task: Compute (base^exp) % mod efficiently in O(log exp) time.
# Expected Goal: Modular Result: 24

base = 2
exp = 10
mod = 1000

# TODO: Write your code below to solve this problem:
problems.buggy_code:

exp = 10
mod = 1000

exp = 10
mod = 1000
res = 1
base = base % mod
while exp > 0:
    if exp % 2 == 1: res = (res * base) % mod
    base = (base * base) % mod
    exp //= 2
print('Modular Result:', res)
